# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to own their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable due to its self-hosted nature, while Slack has limitations on its free plan.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption, while Slack does not have this feature by default.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption
* Customizable and extensible
* Free to use
* Requires technical expertise to set up

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good option for teams who require a wide range of integrations with other tools and services. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations who want to have control over their data and are looking for a self-hosted solution. It's also a good option for teams who require end-to-end encryption and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's data.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your team's needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into Element.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations you need.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its complexity and the technical expertise required to set it up. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element requires a significant amount of server resources to run smoothly, which can be a challenge for smaller teams. However, for teams who value data ownership and control, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching to Element if you have the technical expertise and resources to set it up and maintain it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need many integrations and want to save on costs
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) who require end-to-end encryption and are willing to invest time into setting up Element
* Large teams (more than 50 users) who want to have control over their data and are looking for a self-hosted solution
* Teams who don't need a wide range of integrations with other tools and services
* Teams who are already familiar with self-hosted solutions and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain Element

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any subscription fees. However, you will need to cover the costs of hosting your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element is not as easy to use as Slack, especially for non-technical users. It requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools and services?
Yes, Element has a wide range of integrations available, including integrations with popular tools and services like GitHub and Trello.
### Does Element have end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption, which means that your messages and data are encrypted from end to end and can only be accessed by the intended recipient.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can migrate your Slack data to Element using the Element import tool, which supports importing data from Slack.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer real-time messaging, file sharing, and integration with third-party services, making them ideal for remote teams, enterprises, and communities. The core use case for both platforms is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data, reduce costs, or improve scalability.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Slack offers a free plan with limited features, while Mattermost is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting.
* **Data Ownership**: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* **Setup Complexity**: Slack is generally easier to set up and use, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* **Scalability**: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it a better choice for large teams and enterprises, while Slack's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* **Integration**: Mattermost has a more extensive library of open-source integrations, including support for GitLab and Jenkins, while Slack has a more comprehensive library of commercial integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large library of commercial integrations
* Good mobile app support
* Limited control over data
* Can be expensive for large teams
**Mattermost:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Extensive library of open-source integrations
* More complex setup and configuration
* Limited support for commercial integrations

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of commercial integrations. It's ideal for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay a premium for convenience. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a better choice for large teams and enterprises that require more control over their data, scalability, and customization. It's ideal for teams with technical expertise and a need for open-source integrations.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool like Slack-export.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.
4. Configure your Mattermost integrations and customize your setup as needed.
5. Test your Mattermost setup and migrate your team.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and customization options. However, it's worth noting that Mattermost's scalability can be limited by the underlying infrastructure, and teams may need to invest in additional hardware or expertise to support large-scale deployments. For teams that require full control over their data, scalability, and customization, Mattermost is a clear choice, while teams that prioritize ease of use and commercial integrations may prefer Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with limited budgets that don't need commercial integrations
* Large teams that require full control over their data and scalability
* Enterprises with existing open-source infrastructure and expertise
* Communities that need customization and self-hosting options
* Teams that don't need mobile app support or commercial integrations

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost is free and open-source, allowing teams to self-host their own servers.
### Is Slack more expensive than Mattermost?
Yes, Slack can be more expensive than Mattermost, especially for large teams.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.
### Does Mattermost support commercial integrations?
No, Mattermost has a more limited library of commercial integrations compared to Slack.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Yes, Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, especially those with limited budgets and technical expertise.

# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular Git repository management tools used for version control and collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary to a self-hosted solution or seeking more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free public repositories, while Gitea is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Gitea provides complete data ownership, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Gitea requires more technical expertise for setup, while GitHub is more user-friendly.
* Scalability: GitHub is more scalable due to its large infrastructure, while Gitea's scalability depends on the user's server.
* Integration: GitHub has better integration with other developer tools, while Gitea has limited integration with third-party services.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Pros:
  + Easy to use and set up
  + Large community and extensive documentation
  + Integrates well with other developer tools
  + Scalable infrastructure
  + Free public repositories
* Cons:
  + Limited control over data
  + Costs can add up for large teams
  + Proprietary license
  + Limited customization options
  + Dependence on GitHub's infrastructure
### Gitea
* Pros:
  + Self-hosted and free
  + Complete control over data
  + Customizable
  + Open-source and community-driven
  + Low costs for large teams
* Cons:
  + Steeper learning curve
  + Limited integration with third-party services
  + Requires technical expertise for setup
  + Dependence on user's server infrastructure
  + Limited scalability compared to GitHub

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for teams of any size that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and integration with other developer tools. It's ideal for teams that don't require complete control over their data and are willing to pay for the convenience. On the other hand, Gitea is perfect for teams that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise and a self-hosted infrastructure.

Gitea is also a good choice for teams that require complete control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing their repository management tool. For large teams, Gitea can be a cost-effective solution, as it eliminates per-user costs. However, teams that rely heavily on integration with third-party services may find GitHub a better fit.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which provides a ZIP archive of your repository's data.
2. Set up your Gitea server and create a new repository.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to import your GitHub repository data into your new Gitea repository.
4. Update your repository settings, such as permissions and collaborators, to match your Gitea setup.
5. Verify that all your data has been successfully migrated and that your Gitea repository is functioning as expected.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a self-hosted solution with complete control over data. However, it's essential to consider the technical expertise required for setup and the potential limitations in scalability and integration with third-party services. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Gitea's search functionality can be limited compared to GitHub's.

Gitea's community-driven approach and open-source license make it an attractive option for teams that value customization and cost-effectiveness. However, teams that rely heavily on integration with other developer tools may find GitHub a better fit. Ultimately, the choice between GitHub and Gitea depends on your team's specific needs and priorities.

For teams that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness, Gitea is an excellent choice. On the other hand, teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and integration with other developer tools may prefer GitHub. We recommend that small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise consider switching to Gitea, while larger teams or those with complex integration requirements may want to stick with GitHub.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require integration with third-party services
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that value data ownership and customization
* Teams with limited budgets that want to reduce costs
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle self-hosted setup and maintenance
* Teams that don't require advanced scalability and can manage their own infrastructure

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between GitHub and Gitea?
The main difference between GitHub and Gitea is that GitHub is a proprietary, cloud-based solution, while Gitea is a self-hosted, open-source alternative. Gitea provides complete control over data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.

### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is free and open-source. It can be self-hosted, eliminating per-user costs.

### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, you can migrate your GitHub repository to Gitea using the GitHub export tool and the Gitea import tool.

### Does Gitea have the same features as GitHub?
Gitea has many of the same features as GitHub, including repository management, issue tracking, and project management. However, Gitea's features may not be as polished or extensive as GitHub's.

### Is Gitea suitable for large teams?
Gitea can be suitable for large teams, but it depends on the team's specific needs and infrastructure. Gitea's scalability and integration with third-party services may be limited compared to GitHub.
